newsitem.title: LAOS: Laos says NT2 dam best option for power needs.
newsitem.headline: Laos says NT2 dam best option for power needs.

text.p: Lao officials said on Saturday they saw few viable alternatives to a controversial proposed $1.5 billion hydroelectric dam and suggested that other energy options could have dire environmental and social consequences.

During the third and final day of consultation on alternatives to the Nam Theun 2 (NT2), they said the dam -- due to generate a maximum of 900 megawatts -- and other planned hydropower projects were likely to be the country's best option to meet the power needs of the nation.

Vice Minister of Industry and Handicrafts Khammone Phonekeo said: "Hydropower development could contribute to the protection of the environment," by reducing reliance on the timber industry and slash-and-burn agriculture.
Laos has promised to provide 3,000 MW of power by 2006 to the Electricity Generating Authority of Thailand (EGAT) and between 1,500 and 2,000 MW of power to Vietnam between 1998 and 2006.

It can meet those needs without new hydropower projects through coal-fired plants, but that route will likely prove more environmentally destructive, said Engelbertus Oud, project manager of the alternatives study.
Laos oroduces about 1,000 to 2,000 tonnes of coal a year.

While the Lao government appeared determined to pursue the hydropower option, some dissenters at the consultation expressed concerns about the NT2's toll on a 450-sq-km (170-sq-mile) site to be flooded, an adjacent conservation area and the proposed resettlement of 1,000 families.
Others suggested smaller dams or run-of-river dams which do not create reservoirs could be other options.
The Lao government will have to examine those concerns as part of the study into alternative options and the economic, social and environmental impact of the proposals.

The World Bank, which is considering $100 million in vital loan guarantees to the project, has said those studies and more public hearings will have to be carried out before it makes a decision on the loan.

The Nam Theun II Electricity Consortium (NTEC), which is developing the project, includes Transfield Corp, Electricite de France, Italian-Thai Development, Thailand's Jasmine International and Phatra Thanakit.
NTEC has said it will pull out of the project unless it gets the $100 million in loan guarantees from the World Bank.
